newsitem.title: CANADA: Reuters poll shows Canadian Liberals unshaken.
newsitem.headline: Reuters poll shows Canadian Liberals unshaken.

text.p: Prime Minister Jean Chretien's Liberals have maintained a virtually unshakable lead in the polls as Canada's election campaign heads into its final week, a Reuters poll released on Sunday showed.
The poll, conducted by Zogby International, showed the Liberal lead nationally dropping by only one point to a little less than 24 points in the nine days since the last Reuters-Zogby survey.

The Liberals led with 43.8 percent of decided voters to 20.2 percent for the Conservatives and 16.9 percent for Reform, two parties splitting the right wing. New Democrats take 10.6 percent, the separatist Bloc Quebecois 6.6 percent.
"Chretien is surely on the way to a big win," pollster John Zogby commented.

The Liberal leader called the June 2 election 1-1/2 years before he had to, and while the Conservatives and Reform have chipped away at his solid lead, neither has broken away from the pack to threaten the Liberal majority in Parliament.

Conservative leader Jean Charest has widely been perceived to have won televised debates the week of May 18, and his charismatic optimism about keeping Canada together has boosted his support in Quebec and Atlantic Canada but failed so far to translate into a national breakthrough.

"While Charest's numbers have improved ... no party has scored the gains they need to make among the disaffected voters -- those who feel the country is headed in the wrong direction, and the jobless," Zogby said.
For the first time this campaign, less than a majority (46 percent) feel the country is heading in the right direction, while 33 percent feel it is on the wrong track.
But among those who feel it is on the wrong track, Reform and Conservatives each get 26 percent support and the Liberals and New Democrats 18 percent each.

Nonetheless, if Charest's momentum holds in Quebec, the Conservatives can hope at least to do substantially better than the dismal showing in the 1993 election, when they were slashed from a majority to only two out of 295 seats.

The poll confirms increasing softness of the separatist vote in mainly French-speaking Quebec, two years after the province came within 1 percentage point of voting for independence in a bitterly fought referendum.
Among those who were decided, 58.4 percent said they would vote against sovereignty if the same question were posed today, while only 41.6 percent said they would vote for it.

This was mirrored in continued weakness of the Bloc Quebecois, which took 49 percent of the vote in 1993 and 54 out of 75 Quebec seats. The Reuters poll put them now at only 27 percent in Quebec, tied with the Conservatives and trailing the Liberals at 38 percent.
The margin of error for the national sample of 1,005, taken on May 22-24, is 3.2 percentage points, while for Quebec it is 6.0 and for Ontario 5.2.
It was Ontario, with 103 out of the 301 seats in the next Parliament, that looked as if it could guarantee Chretien re-election.

The Liberals seized all but one seat in 1993, and Charest and Reform leader Preston Manning have spent more time there this campaign than anywhere else, yet the Liberal lead is virtually unchanged at 55 percent to 19 percent for the Conservatives and 15 percent for Reform.
Outside Toronto, Chretien's Ontario support is marginally softer but still far ahead of his rivals.

Chretien, who ran on a platform of "Jobs, jobs, jobs" in 1993, spent much of his mandate slashing government spending and bringing the deficit under control -- regaining financial market respect and leading to interest rate declines.

He has campaigned now for the chance to spend more money when budget surpluses start rolling in in a few years, deriding Conservative and Reform calls for broad tax cuts and New Democrat calls for higher taxes on business and the rich.

The left-leaning Toronto Star, Canada's biggest newspaper, endorsed Chretien on Saturday, saying they deserve another chance, while the politically more conservative Sun chain plumped for Charest on Sunday.

The reason, it said, was to boot the Bloc Quebecois from official opposition, a position it held since it had the second largest number of seats. It also advocated joining Reform and the Conservatives to avoid the split of the right.
